title: Song: To Celia
short: Printed as the ninth poem of The Forest in Jonson's 1616 Works, this is a lyric meant for singing and later one of the best-known English songs.
body: The poem appeared as 'Song. To Celia' (The Forest 9) in the folio Workes of 1616. 'Celia' (from Latin caelum, heaven) is a stock name for a mistress in Latin and Renaissance love poetry; Jonson also uses it in Volpone's seduction song 'Come, my Celia' (Forest 5). The poem is less a confession than a display of craft: two eight-line stanzas building a single compliment, that the lady is more divine than wine and more fragrant than roses. Its fame grew in the eighteenth century, when it was set to a tune of uncertain origin (often attributed, without proof, to various composers; John Wall Callcott is believed by some to have composed it as a glee around 1790); in that form it became a parlour and drinking song.

title: Philostratus' love letters
short: Almost every conceit is taken from the erotic prose letters of the Greek sophist Philostratus (third century AD), recombined into a new song.
body: Richard Cumberland pointed out in The Observer in 1791, and J. A. Symonds demonstrated in 1884, that the poem stitches together phrases from several of Philostratus' love letters: one asks the beloved to drink only with her eyes, or to put her lips to the cup and fill it with kisses; others describe a rose wreath sent not to honour the beloved but so that the roses might not wither, and ask her to send it back smelling of herself. The letters are numbered differently in different editions (RPO cites them as XXIV, XXX and XXXI). Hoeniger calls the poem little more than a skilled cento; George Burke Johnston preferred to describe it as a synthesis of scattered passages. Either way, Jonson's art lies in turning loose Greek prose into tight English song, a typical example of his classical 'imitation'.

title: pledge
short: To 'pledge' is to drink to someone in answer to their toast; the lovers exchange looks as drinkers exchange healths.
body: In the drinking ritual of the period one person drank a health and the other 'pledged' it by drinking in return (OED, pledge, v., sense of drinking in response to a toast). The conceit makes glances into wine: if Celia drinks to him with her eyes, he will answer with his. The image belongs to the Petrarchan tradition in which love enters through the eyes, but here it is made convivial and social rather than painful. The next couplet offers an alternative: a kiss left on the rim of the cup will be enough, and he will not need wine at all.

anchor: a kiss but in the cup
title: a kiss in the cup
short: If she touches the cup with her lips, the kiss she leaves will intoxicate him more than wine.
body: This is the second half of the Philostratean letter Jonson is following, in which the lover asks the beloved to fill the cup with kisses instead of wine. 'But' here means 'only': she need do no more than leave a kiss. The line also recalls the ancient practice of lovers drinking from the side of the cup the other has touched (a motif in Ovid, Amores 1.4.31-32, and the Greek Anthology). The point is that her slightest gesture surpasses the real drink.

title: thirst of the soul
short: The soul's thirst asks for a 'divine' drink: the lover's desire is spiritualised, raised above bodily appetite.
body: The second quatrain turns from the cup to the soul. A thirst that rises from the soul cannot be satisfied by wine; it asks for something divine. The phrasing borrows the Platonic and Christian language of spiritual thirst (compare Psalm 42:2, 'My soul thirsteth for God'), but uses it as gallant compliment: the divine drink is the lady herself. The tension between the sacred vocabulary and the secular wooing is typical of Renaissance love lyric and gives the stanza its lift before the final hyperbole.

title: Jove's nectar
short: Nectar was the drink of the Olympian gods; even Jupiter's own cup would not tempt him to give up hers.
body: In Greek myth the gods drink nectar and eat ambrosia, which keep them immortal (Homer, Iliad 1.598, Odyssey 5.93). 'Might I of Jove's nectar sup' means 'even if I could drink Jupiter's nectar'. The 1616 folio prints 'Ioves', and because the capital I and J were not yet distinguished in print, later texts sometimes misread the word as 'Love's', which changes the sense; the archive's 'Jove's' is the correct reading. The stanza ends on the classic hyperbole of the lover who would refuse immortality for his mistress.

anchor: I would not change for thine
title: change for
short: 'Change for' means give in exchange for: he would not trade her drink for the gods' nectar.
body: The idiom is the older sense of 'change' as 'exchange' (OED, change, v., to give or take in exchange). The line is grammatically compressed: 'I would not change [thine] for [it]' or 'I would not change [it] for thine'. Readers have noticed that the words can be read either way; most editors take it that he would not exchange her cup even for Jove's nectar, which is the natural sense of the climax. The neat monosyllables give the stanza a firm close.

title: the rosy wreath
short: 'Late' means lately; the gift of a rose garland, a traditional love token, was meant to preserve the roses rather than honour her.
body: The second stanza takes up another Philostratean letter, in which the lover sends roses so that they might not wither when touched by the beloved. The wreath (a chaplet of roses, worn at feasts in the classical world) is a carpe diem emblem of fading beauty, but Jonson reverses its usual moral: instead of reminding the lady that she will fade like the roses, he imagines her as the source of the roses' immortality. 'Not so much honouring thee' is a witty, almost impudent, qualification: the compliment is greater for pretending to be smaller.

title: her breath
short: She merely breathed on the wreath and sent it back; ever since, it smells not of roses but of her.
body: The lady's response looks like a rejection (she returns the gift), but the poem turns it into a miracle: her breath has entered the roses, which now grow and give off her scent rather than their own. The closing 'Not of itself, but thee' answers 'Not so much honouring thee' in l. 10, completing a chiasmus across the stanza. In Philostratus the lover asks for the roses back for this very reason. Some readers find a quiet melancholy under the wit: the lover keeps only a token of a lady who has refused him.

anchor: The thirst that from the soul
title: metre and rhyme
short: Alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter lines (common measure), in two octaves rhyming abcbabcb, give the poem its song-like movement.
body: Each stanza alternates eight- and six-syllable lines, the 'common measure' of hymns and ballads, which made it easy to set to music. Only the even lines rhyme across the whole octave (mine/wine/divine/thine; thee/be/me/thee), while the odd lines rhyme in pairs across the quatrains (eyes/rise, cup/sup; wreath/breathe, there/swear): RPO gives the scheme as abcbabcb. The repeated long -ine rhyme of the first stanza is itself musical, linking the lover's 'mine' to the lady's 'thine' through 'wine' and 'divine'. The indentation of the even lines in the archive text reflects this alternation.
